text: Cassini came from Earth, and an abandoned orbit could slowly decay. If the spacecraft ended up hitting a moon, it would carry Earth material, possibly microbes or organic particles, onto a world like Enceladus, where scientists think a liquid water ocean might exist. Crashing it into Saturn's upper atmosphere made it burn up, taking it out of the system. That removed the chance of it eventually landing on a moon. It also kept the end of the mission clean for future probes. For a mission studying moons, that mattered: even a tiny amount of Earth biology could change what we find later.

Your stationary leg is not actually doing nothing. While the pushing leg moves, the other leg is doing the hard work of keeping you on the board. It has to stay planted, take the weight of your body, absorb the small bumps, and hold your balance. If that leg is already sore, stiff, or injured, the pressure and vibration from riding can make it hurt. The board itself is not very forgiving, and repeated impacts travel up through the foot, ankle, knee and hip. If you have a problem in one of those areas, a skate session can make it feel worse.

What you would notice is usually a dull ache or a sharp catch when you start moving or stop. That kind of pain often points to the leg being overloaded rather than a new injury. If the pain only happens when the leg is the stationary one, it is worth checking whether you are putting too much weight on it or holding a stiff posture. Many people find that the stationary leg is doing more balancing than they expect, especially if the pushing leg is doing most of the work. You can reduce the load by keeping your weight centered, bending your knees a little, and not locking the joint. If the leg has a known issue, such as a sprained ankle or tight hip, skateboarding can aggravate it. In that case, a short session, a good pair of shoes, and a softer landing surface help. If the pain is sudden, severe, or accompanied by swelling, it is the kind of thing to have looked at by someone who can examine the leg. In a thread, I would say the stationary leg hurts because it is carrying the load, absorbing shocks, and holding your balance on the board.

It isn't a statement about where they live now or where their passports say. The term is about ancestry. African American usually means someone with ancestors from Africa, and that can be many generations back. A person might have lived in the United States for a hundred years, yet the label still points to African roots.

I think the confusion comes from mixing up nationality and descent. Being from Africa and being of African descent are different things. The name is not saying everyone in the group is currently from the continent. It is a historical and cultural marker.

Most Black Americans trace their ancestry to Africa, often through the transatlantic slave trade. That history is why the label sticks even when people have no living connection to the continent. It is a way of acknowledging where their lineage came from.

Some people prefer African American, others Afro-American, and still others simply say Black American. The word Africa in the name is a reference to origin, not a claim that the person has recently come from there.

I would not read the term as a geographic location. It is a genealogical and cultural description, and that is the point.

Crossing into Syria from Turkey or Iraq, you see trucks rolling in with crates of AK-47s and RPGs. Much of it moves through black markets in Aleppo or via smugglers using the same routes as the drug and fuel trades. You can walk into a shop in the old city and buy a used rifle off the shelf. The arms keep coming because the central government cannot hold its borders, and local clans are still settling scores. For a lot of families, keeping a rifle in the house is just the local way of making sure they survive.

I'd say the word drug is doing a lot of work here. It covers insulin, ibuprofen, and the medicines you take for blood pressure, none of which people call bad. So the question is really about drugs that produce strong pleasure, not about medicines in general.

If you use heroin or cocaine, the most noticeable thing is that the effect does not stay the same. The first dose feels very different from the fifth or tenth. That is the brain changing its set point. A strong reward signal makes the nervous system adapt, so the same amount stops giving the same high. This is tolerance, and it is also what pulls people toward using more. Dependence is not a character flaw. It is the brain trying to keep things steady while being flooded with an abnormal reward signal. Think of it like a phone screen. If you keep turning the brightness up, your eyes adapt and the same setting feels dimmer.

A drug with intense euphoria and literally zero adverse effects is not impossible as an idea. But in practice, the same circuits that make a person feel great are the ones that get recalibrated. The body also has to process and clear the substance, and that involves the liver, the heart, and the rest of the system. You can make a drug milder or safer, and researchers have been trying for decades. Still, the stronger the immediate pleasure, the harder it is to keep every other effect at zero. So a milder version can still feel different day to day. The body has to break it down and clear it. You can design for less dependence, but you cannot make the reward system ignore itself.

What people usually do is use a little at first, then use more to get the same feeling. That is where the worry becomes real. The drug is not secretly evil. The problem is the mismatch between a very strong artificial reward and a nervous system built for food, sex, and social connection. If the reward is too strong, the system compensates. So a perfectly safe euphoria drug would still have to deal with tolerance, dependence, and the body's cleanup work. It is not a contradiction to have a useful drug. It is much harder to have a very rewarding one that leaves no mark.

Hi,
I know that pain is real, and it is not just in your head. A long shopping trip can put your body under a lot of stress, since you are on your feet in crowds and heat for hours. That combination can make you feel drained, tense, or get a headache that does not feel like your usual ones. Dehydration or going without enough food can make it worse. I would not keep pushing through it. Give yourself water, a short break, and a snack. If the pain keeps coming back, see your doctor and get it checked.
Thanks

Hi,

I think your brother's little test got your attention into word associations. When he asked what cows drink, the idea of cows immediately brought milk to mind, because that is the most common association most people have with cows. Saying silk several times probably made you more sensitive to how words and concepts connect. It is not a mistake in your knowledge. You know cows drink water, but the question activated a stronger, more automatic thought. That kind of response is normal, and it tells you more about attention and associations than about memory. I would not worry about it. The repeated word game is not really about silk. It is about how quickly related ideas pop into mind. Your answer shows the milk idea was more available than water at that moment. If you asked him again, he might say water, and the testing would make the correct answer feel more familiar.

Thanks

Hi,

Thanks for the note. You didn't list the questions, so I'll cover the parts people ask about most.

The first thing is what you can actually afford, not just what you want. That usually means monthly payments, taxes, insurance, maintenance, and closing costs. People often get surprised by the costs around buying, and I would not sign anything before knowing those numbers.

If you are considering a specific place, get an independent inspection. I would not skip it even if the seller says everything is fine. You are buying a building, not a photo. A good inspector can point out roof, plumbing, electrical, or foundation problems that affect price or whether you walk away.

For the mortgage side, get preapproval before touring homes. That gives you a realistic ceiling and helps you compare loans. I would also read the fine print on rate, fees, and what happens if rates move. If unsure, ask the lender to explain fixed and adjustable terms in plain language.

Don't let a deadline push you into a bad decision. Buying a house is a long commitment, and the best offers are the ones you can live with.

Thanks

Hi,
That sounds like a product you are actually using, so I would start with your own routine. A 3-in-1 has to clean skin, hair, and hair ends with one formula, while a 2-in-1 only has to manage hair cleansing and conditioning. That is the practical difference.

What you will notice is that a 3-in-1 usually has a milder, more water-soluble formula so it can rinse from skin as well as hair. It cannot be as strong as separate shampoo, and it cannot give the same depth of care as separate conditioner. A 2-in-1 can be more concentrated on hair, but it still does not address the rest of the body.

For your case, if your hair is dry or you want real conditioning, a 3-in-1 is a convenience product, not a full substitute. You may need a separate conditioner or leave-in. In a quick shower, it saves time and products. If your hair is damaged, you are better off using separate shampoo and conditioner. I would not pay for a 3-in-1 if I wanted a serious hair treatment. It is fine for an ordinary wash, while damaged hair needs more. The difference is a compromise in strength and purpose.

Thanks

Hi,

You can measure continental motion in a few different ways, and the most direct is to put GPS receivers on solid rock and track them over months or years. The receivers report their latitude, longitude, and height, and when the same point drifts by a few centimeters a year, that is the speed of the land beneath it. It is not about the whole continent moving like a solid block. Different parts move at different rates, so people set up arrays of stations and look at differences between them.

For longer time scales, geologists compare the rocks and fossils on separated landmasses, look at matching coastlines, and read the magnetic stripes left in ocean floor rocks. Those clues say how far continents have moved since they were together, and when you pair that distance with the age of the rocks, you get an average speed. The ocean floor gives the cleanest record because new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and carries magnetic patterns with it.

None of this is as simple as watching a coastline slide. You need many observations, repeated measurements, and careful comparison of geological records. The two approaches check each other, so both are used.

Thanks

First cousin marriages are a common way inbreeding shows up. The main issue is that relatives often carry the same rare harmful recessive mutations. When two closely related people have a child, the child is more likely to inherit two copies of the same bad variant, one from each parent. This is called increased homozygosity. Geneticists measure this with the inbreeding coefficient, an estimate of how much shared ancestry increases homozygosity and risk.

Many of these variants affect brain development and therefore cognitive ability. Inbred offspring often score lower on IQ tests. The effect is probabilistic, not guaranteed. Each child has a higher chance of inheriting harmful recessive genes, but not every child is affected. Environmental factors also matter, so the science is about genetics plus upbringing. The closer the relationship, the higher the chance of harm, especially for recessive mutations. This risk grows with closer kinship and more generations.

When a limb is injured, the pain is real, but it usually feels less severe than an injury to the torso, head, or groin. The arm has muscle and bone that spread the impact, and the limb is not packed with the vital organs that make trunk injuries feel so threatening. Pain is not just a physical signal. If the body senses a threat to survival, it can release adrenaline and other chemicals that dull the immediate pain, and the person may also mentally compare the injury to less dangerous spots. A cut in the arm may be alarming, but it does not usually trigger the same fear of losing consciousness, breathing, or fertility. The exact amount of pain depends on the wound, the person, and how much blood is lost. That combination of physical padding and lower perceived danger makes arm injuries often seem less painful than injuries elsewhere.

Carbon monoxide is the gas that quietly builds up in a garage where a car has been idling, or around a generator running in a closed room. The danger is not that the gas itself burns the lungs. It is that red blood cells use hemoglobin to carry oxygen, and carbon monoxide grabs that hemoglobin much more tightly than oxygen does. Once a person breathes it, the gas takes the oxygen's place and stays there. The body keeps moving, but the blood is no longer carrying enough oxygen for the brain and muscles.

Carbon dioxide is a different case. It is the gas we exhale, and normal levels are part of everyday breathing. It does not compete with oxygen for the same spot in the blood in the way carbon monoxide does. Rooms can have the usual amount of CO2 without anyone feeling ill, for most people. At high concentrations, though, CO2 can make it hard to breathe and can cause dizziness, headache, or loss of consciousness, so it is not harmless in every amount. The contrast is practical: CO is dangerous even at low concentrations because it blocks oxygen transport, while CO2 is only a breathing problem when it accumulates to a high level.

For the office wiki, the useful point is that carbon monoxide is hard to detect. It is colorless, odorless, and silent. In a building, it can come from a car in a garage, a gas appliance, or an unvented heater. The practical response is to keep fuel-burning equipment ventilated, use a CO detector near sleeping areas, and treat any detector alarm as a reason to get outside and check the source. People often mistake it for a bad flu. A detector gives an early warning before symptoms become obvious, and symptoms can be easy to miss.

If you are told to brace for impact, you should get into the position before the crew asks, not during the jolt. Put your feet flat on the floor, lean your body forward, and bring your hands to protect your face and head. The point is to stop your body from continuing forward when the plane stops suddenly. Your head and chest are the parts that can hit the seat or floor, and the brace position keeps them from doing that. It also helps keep your spine and neck from bending sharply. If you are seated, keep your back against the seat and your chin toward your chest.

You do not need to perform a perfect athletic move. The idea is simple: lower your center of gravity, keep your limbs under control, and shield your face. In a crash or hard landing, most serious injuries come from the body moving and striking the cabin. Bracing reduces that risk. It will not make the crash feel softer, but it can keep you from adding your own injuries to the situation. Do not worry about looking coordinated; the crew only needs you to be still and protected. If the crew gives the command, take the position early and hold it until told to release.

Many old businesses did exist, but they rarely survived as independent brands. Before industrialization, most companies depended on local demand, personal relationships, and manual skills. When factories, railroads, and mass distribution arrived, smaller operators were often bought out or squeezed out. A few pre-industrial firms still exist, but their original identities faded as they expanded and reorganized. The businesses most people recognize today are either very old institutions that changed completely or newer firms built for the industrial age.

I kept seeing dealership ads with rates lower than the bank, so I assumed I was doing something wrong. Then I sat down with the actual numbers and the picture changed. The rate is not the price. A bank loan may carry a higher interest rate, but the dealer's total cost can be higher once you include their fees and payment structure.

At the dealership, I was offered a low rate tied to a package that included an extended warranty and roadside assistance. The salesperson said the package was optional, but the rate discount depended on taking it. I could take the low rate only if I paid for extras I did not need. At the bank, I could get a loan with no extras and a payment I could choose myself. The difference was not just the rate. It was the whole package.

I looked at a 48-month loan for a car in my price range. The dealer quoted 4.9%, which looked better than the bank's 6.2%. But the dealer added a $750 documentation fee, a $1,200 service package that was optional, and a payment that started high and stayed high. The bank had no required add-ons and let me choose a level payment. Over the life of the loan, the dealer package cost me more than the bank, even with the lower advertised rate.

What I noticed is that dealerships often use the low rate as a hook. The rate makes you sit at the table, and then the fees do the work. A bank is usually simpler: you see the interest rate, you see the fee, you sign. No optional packages, no surprise add-ons.

My position is that the advertised rate is a starting point, not the answer. If you compare only the rate, the dealer wins on paper. If you compare the total amount paid over the loan term, the bank can win easily. The dealer's lower rate is real, but it is not the only number that matters.

Most people I know only look at the rate and sign whatever the dealer puts in front of them. I would not do that anymore. I would get the bank loan, compare the total paid over the term, and let the numbers decide. I would also ask the bank for the total amount due at the end of the term. That is how I ended up financing through the bank.

I find the patchwork of marijuana laws in US states both practical and frustrating. Some states have legalized recreational use, others allow medical use, and a few still treat possession as a crime. I support letting states choose their own rules, because a one-size-fits-all federal law would ignore how differently regions think about cannabis. The concrete problem is what happens between states. If you drive from a legal state to a stricter state with a small amount, you may be fine or you may be in trouble, and the difference can mean a ticket or a misdemeanor. I would prefer a clearer federal baseline that protects people using marijuana legally under state law, while leaving states room to set their own limits. For me, the real issue is predictability, and I want people who drive across state lines to know what is allowed where they are.

My knee aches after long walks, and I keep thinking about the small electrical signals that make it move. Nerves do not carry electricity the way a wire does. They use ions, mostly sodium and potassium, moving across cell membranes. When a nerve fires, sodium floods in, the inside briefly turns positive, and the signal jumps down the axon like a row of dominoes falling. Muscles respond because their own membranes change ion flow, causing contraction. The whole process is powered by cells pumping ions back into place. It is a chemical current, the kind your body runs on every second.

Most people picture sampling as cutting a famous line out of an old record and pasting it into a new track. In my view, that misses the point. For me, sampling is about finding an emotional color that a live performance cannot quite give you, and then doing the slow work of making it sit inside your own song.

I keep coming back to a simple idea: a sample is not just a snippet. It is a piece of recorded time. When I look through old records, I am not hunting for a melody I can lift. I am listening for a voice cracking, a bass line with dirt on it, a drummer hitting the offbeat in a way that a modern session player might not. Those details are hard to reproduce, and that is why they matter.

In practice, the process is messier than the final result suggests. You find a recording, record the few seconds you want into a digital audio workstation, then chop it into short pieces. You change the pitch, stretch the timing, add reverb, and layer it under your own drums and bass. The hard part is not the cutting. The hard part is making the borrowed sound stop sounding borrowed. If it still feels like a quote, the track falls apart.

There is also the business side. If you use someone else’s master recording, you generally need to clear rights with the owner of the master and the publisher of the underlying composition. That can be expensive and slow. I have heard too many stories of producers finishing a track only to find the clearance cost eating the whole budget. So some artists sample in the public domain or use material they own, while others pay for the privilege.

What I respect about sampling is its honesty. It says: I want this exact sound, this exact moment, not a copy of it. A sample carries the room, the microphone, the age of the tape. That is a kind of authenticity a fresh recording cannot provide. But authenticity is not enough. The sample has to serve the song, not the other way around.

My position is simple: sampling is borrowing a feeling. The skill is in restraint. A good sample disappears into the track. A bad sample sits on top of it like a sticker. I prefer the ones that make you feel the old record was always part of the new song.

I keep getting headaches, and I think the answer is simpler than people assume. My head does not hurt because the brain is damaged. The brain has almost no pain receptors. The pain comes from the sensitive membranes, blood vessels and muscles around it. When I am tired, dehydrated or tense, those structures can swell or contract, and that is what you feel as pressure or throbbing. For me, a headache usually starts as a dull band around the forehead, then tightens. I notice it after sitting too long at a desk, skipping water, or sleeping badly. The practical part is that the head is reporting something else, like stress, low fluid, or poor rest. So I stop treating the pain as a mysterious brain problem and look at the day before. I treat it as a warning, not a medical crisis. Most days, I can usually spot the trigger.

I can’t tell you if the food is good because we never got to eat. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, choosing this place specifically because our 10:00 p.m. show was in the same hotel, so we figured it would be easy. We entered our names into their completely useless digital waitlist and were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, but stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn’t be seated until 9:15 p.m. It was a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait extends that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn’t completely wasted. I would give zero stars if that were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. I figured before going that the price would be comparable to a steakhouse, but afterward I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I expected to pay at one.

I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but I feel like you can find those at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

Overall, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

Four stars, keeping it. The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of my thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key repeats now and then, so “example” becomes “eexample” and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I’m typing fast and not looking. I paid $38 and kept it anyway because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had pulled off a keycap and found out myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison. My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don’t ache by the end anymore. That mattered more to me than the rattle. Sending it back would have meant paying postage and boxing it up, and I would have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been to Vegas for most of my life, well, the under-21 version, so I’ve sat through plenty of shows before I could gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

The circular stage is actually smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too. The strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are serious athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not exactly a rip-off, just that if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

The problem is clarity. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, there’s way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit much harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, where more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave feeling overwhelmed.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by phone. They never arrived because the sales rep wrote the address wrong: her handwritten 7 was read as a 1. The address should have been 5407, but the package went to 5401. The residents there took it to the local UPS store to send it back. It disappeared, and we never heard from it again. We did not know for several weeks. While the dispute was going on, we put in another order for two shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the first two. The owner took it from there. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong address, but said no refund until the shirts came back. He said we were partly to blame because we had not been friendly enough to the residents at 5401, who lived four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company, eventually got a credit.
